utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. There are no preliminaries, as far as I understand, which means that, in order to conclude the testimony of the present witness, we move into closed session. And, Mr. Stojanovic, could you give us an indication as to how much time you'd still need so that the public is aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe it's going to be in accordance with what I had announced; that is to say, another 45 minutes, up to one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Lukic, we take the break now, that is the sort break after one hour, because I have not heard of any request to return to the two breaks, each 30 minutes schedule. So up to that moment we will follow the schedule as we usually did. Is the Prosecution ready after -- yes, I think Mr. Mladic wants to consult with you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Groome, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness after the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would require protective measures. That's Witness RM083.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There are no protective measures for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No protective measure and that would be Witness RM083 -- 53, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, perhaps you use the break to consult with your client. We take a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could take this opportunity to introduce the Chamber to a new member of staff that's appearing for the first time. That's Mr. Edward Jeremy. He will be taking the next witness, Adil Medic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, welcome into court, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that 45 minutes are needed for the next witness. Then I suggest -- I do not know whether in the session after that the cross-examination could be concluded?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, we established two hours for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So probably we should finish by the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that would be possible, then at least the witness could be released and could return home again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the witness is brought in perhaps I might deal with a few preliminary matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Firstly regarding adjudicated facts. The Prosecution will not adduce all the evidence that this witness can provide in reliance on the following adjudicated facts: 460, 461, 463, 465, 468, 469, 470, 471, 472, 473, 476, 478, 487, and 1006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That corresponds with the list we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, there might be some instances in my examination where my question are aimed at eliciting evidence that overlaps partly with an adjudicated fact, and on these occasions in order to assist the Chamber, I will endeavour to indicate that at the appropriate point in my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And try to avoid it to the extent possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: As regards associated exhibits, there are no associated exhibits relating to this witness. But I will tender exhibits shown to the witness at the time that they are dealt with during the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, regarding the witness's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there's any need, otherwise I would first now address the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Medic. Can you hear me in a language you understand? See you're nodding yes, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Medic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration of which the text will be handed out to you now by the usher. I would like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Medic. Please be seated. Mr. Medic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Jeremy. Mr. Jeremy is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Jeremy, to the extent the preliminaries need attention, then you weave them in -- in your examination, I take it, or address the Court --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- at the appropriate moment. Please proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Can I ask you to please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Adil Medic, born in Sanica, municipality of Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, is it true that you have previously provided written statements to the Office of the Prosecutor and testified before this Tribunal in another trial?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I show the witness his statement, regarding the 1996 statement this was without paragraph numbering. As with the last witness statement, as with the last witness, these paragraphs have been numbered by a member of the OTP staff and the numbered version uploaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think we can use the now-numbered -- paragraph-numbered statement, Mr. Lukic, unless you have any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since it was numbered, I numbered it myself, page by page. But I will try to follow -- and I don't have that numbered version with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll ask my staff to bring one to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, you can produce it on your screen if that's the version uploaded and then take it from e-court as we usually do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thanks. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, just still on the statement, at various points in my examination of Mr. Medic I refer to his 1996 statement as well as his 2001 statement. And for efficiency, I think Mr. Medic would be assisted, if I could, with your leave, provide him with a hard copy of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. With the numbered paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please provide Mr. Medic with a hard copy of his statement -- statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor which you signed on 31 January 1996?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And did you also provide a statement which you signed on 9 November 2001 which corrected certain inaccuracies in the statement you signed on 31 January 1996?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were certain corrections made, more of a technical nature, not exactly substantive. Perhaps it had to do with terms, and that's quite logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I ask that 65 ter 28356 be brought up on our screens. It is a statement of Mr. Medic dated 31 January 1996. I would like the witness to be shown the English language version of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, once the document is on the screen before you, can I ask you if the signature at the bottom of e-court page 1, is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And can I ask that we go to the last page of this statement, e-court page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, is that your signature at the top of the page?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask that 65 ter 28357 be brought up on our screens. It is a supplemental statement of Mr. Medic dated 9 November 2001. This time I would like the witness to be shown the B/C/S version of his statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: To confirm, Mr. Medic, the signature on page 1 of that document is your signature?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And can we go to e-court page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, have you had an opportunity to read and review both your 31 January 1996 statement and your 9 November 2001 statement in preparation for your appearances here today?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Taking those two statements together, did you have any additions, corrections, clarifications or other changes which you wish to make to either statement?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Only with regard to the term related to the suffering of Omer Filipovic. I think the date is wrong. All the rest is fine; these corrections notwithstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And which date did you wish to clarify, Mr. Medic, in relation to Omer Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Omer Filipovic passed away between the 28th and the 29th of July. And I think that the reference here is wrong because it's a day later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Medic. If I were today to ask you questions similar to those that you were asked in the taking of these statements, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And now that you have taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm the truthfulness and accuracy of these statements taken together?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Certainly, I affirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I now tender pursuant to Rule 92 ter Mr. Medic's statement dated 31 January 1996, 65 ter 28356, together with his statement dated 9 November 2001, 65 ter 28357 as the next public Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the 1996 statement would receive number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28356 becomes Exhibit P154, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. The 2001 supplemental statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28357 becomes Exhibit P155, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence under that number. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours with your leave I will now read a short summary of Mr. Medic's written evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Adil Medic was economist who volunteered for the Islamic association in 1991. This was one of a group of organisations, humanitarian organisations, that combined to form the Muslim corps in 1992 after the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mr. Medic was chosen as the leader of the Muslim corps commission in charge of Manjaca camp and specifically prisoner related problems there. On the 18th of June, 1992, Mr. Medic visited Manjaca camp on the invitation of General Talic. Mr. Medic describes the terrible living conditions in the camp which included lack of food, shortage of clothing, and wide speed disease. Mr. Medic spoke to a prison there named Omer Filipovic who told him that the prisoners were regularly beaten. Mr. Medic learnt that at the end of July 1992 Omer Filipovic and Esad Bender were beaten to death in Manjaca camp. On the 22nd of June, 1992, Mr. Medic attended a meeting between Muslim representatives and members of the VRS, including General Talic. At this meeting, Mr. Medic informed General Talic of the inadequate conditions at Manjaca camp and that the civilians there were being ill treated. In all, Mr. Medic made approximately 25 humanitarian visits to Manjaca camp. Mr. Medic also assisted the survivors of the massacre at Vlasic mountain where prisoners were forced to stand at the edge of a cliff and shot in the back. Lastly, Mr. Medic was arrested on the 1st of June, 1995. He was transferred to Mali Logor military prison in Banja Luka where he was beaten on two occasions. He was released on the 29th of December, 1995. Your Honours that concludes my summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please put all the questions you still have to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, paragraphs 1 and 3 of your 1996 statement, Exhibit P154, e-court page 2 in each language, summarise your professional biography. I understand that you retired in 1990 and then volunteered for various humanitarian organisations. Have you been engaged in any other professional activities since you signed that statement in 1996?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Afterwards in August 1996, the association of [indiscernible] of Bosnia-Herzegovina was established and registered with the appropriate authorities. For six years I was vice-president, and after that, I was an editor at the centre for research and documentation. I was involved in research and I also edited what other persons wrote. I spent all of nine years there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In paragraph 6 of your 1996 statement, Exhibit P154, e-court page 2 and 3 in each language, you describe your first visit to Manjaca camp in June 1992 under a military escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, adjudicated facts 460 states that: "The Manjaca camp was run by Bosnian Serb military police under the command of the 1st Krajina Corps and Colonel Bozidar Popovic was the camp commander." I therefore do not intend to lead further evidence directly on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, I will, however, ask a series of general questions about your personal experience of Manjaca camp. Firstly I'd like to show you a sketch of Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I please ask the Court Officer to bring 65 ter 28058 to our screens. It is a sketch of Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, do you recognise the sketch on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes. But the other part of this sketch is missing. I don't know why. This sketch was on a form, A3, and that's where the administrative part is as well in relation to the existing sketch. This only shows the barns where the inmates were, and also the kitchens.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And for the parts of the camp that we can see, is this sketch a fair and accurate depiction of that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: It is an absolutely accurate depiction. The author was very faithful.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, in paragraph 8 of your 1996 statement, Exhibit P154, e-court page 3 in each language, you describe a number of locations that you observed within Manjaca camp. On my instruction, I will ask you to attempt to mark these locations on this sketch, and I would be grateful if the Court Officer could please provide Mr. Medic with a red pen for this purpose. Mr. Medic, without yet marking the image, can you see the kitchen you visited in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the first building on the left-hand side. That was the so-called field kitchen. That's where food was prepared, and that's where they took what they were given to eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Please mark this with a number 1.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, again, without marking the image, can you see the three stables that you indicate housed the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes. The first three stables were full. Prisoners or detainees were there, but there weren't any in the other three, at that point in time; on the 18th of June, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could you please mark the first stable you visited with a number 2.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: The very entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And the second stable you visited with the number 3.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And could you please mark the fourth stable -- excuse me. The third stable that you did not visit with the number 4.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In paragraph 10 of your 1996 statement, Exhibit P154, page 3 in e-court, you refer to your conversation with Manjaca camp prisoner, Omer Filipovic. Without marking the image, can you see on this sketch where that conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: It was outside this basic compound where the inmates were. Roughly here, where these small buildings are. And then opposite them, in a clearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Please mark the location you have just indicated with a number 5.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Lastly, in paragraph 21 of your 1996 statement, Exhibit P154, e-court page 5, you state that in August 1992, prisoners from Omarska camp were transferred to Manjaca. Again, without marking the image, can you see the stables where these persons from Omarska were kept?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: It's the second row, behind the one that I marked, which is practically identical. I mean, physically it is the same. It's the same buildings. It's just a different row.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Please mark that location you've just indicated with a number 6.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: All together?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I now tender this exhibit as marked by Mr. Medic as the next public Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28058 as marked by the witness becomes Exhibit P156, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P15 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, in paragraph 6 of your 1996 statement, Exhibit P154, e-court pages 2 and 3, you state that during that first visit to Manjaca camp, you asked one of your military escorts, a Colonel Tepsic, whether the camp contained exclusively Muslim and Croat prisoners. In response, you state that Colonel Tepsic told you that the prisoners in the camp were all prisoners of war. In paragraph 21 of your statement, e-court page 5, you estimate that at one point four and a half thousand prisoners were in Manjaca. To your knowledge how many of these prisoners that circulated through the camp were prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: I visited Manjaca, and I spoke to officers headed by Colonel Tepsic. When I was given the floor, the first question was whether we were at a collection centre of civilians in Manjaca. His answer was very definite: No, we are in a camp of prisoners of war under the command of the 1st Krajina Corps. When we visited the mentioned-stables, one can conclude that these were civilians only. Some of them wore flip-flops, others were bare-foot, some had only T-shirts on. In this stable, there were about 800 men, and there were no men wearing uniforms. So the logical conclusion was that there were civilians there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: During the course of your approximately 25 visits to the camp did you ever meet a prisoner who was not either Muslim or Croat?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: No. When speaking to the prisoners, they called them prisoners of war, and prisoners of war are captured at the front line, but detainees are persons who are taken from their homes or fields. So they informed me that the persons there were 85 per cent Muslim and 15 per cent Croat. No one ever mentioned any Serbs, and I never saw any either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Before I ask you a few short questions about your access to prisoners in Manjaca camp, I'd now like to show a brief video-clip of footage of a visit to Manjaca camp by British politician, Paddy Ashdown, in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, Ms. Stewart will play the video-clip with 65 ter 22302B using Sanction. For the convenience of all parties, the English and B/C/S transcripts of this video are available in e-court as the same number as -- under the same number as the video-clip. The booths have transcripts of the clip. Unfortunately, the audio can be heard only very faintly but to assist those who cannot hear it English subtitles have been added by the Prosecution. The B/C/S subtitles that appear are from the original footage and were not prepared by the Prosecution. Ms. Stewart, could we now play the clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: "Reporter: Paddy Ashdown had broken his holiday and travelled for three days over a thousand miles to get to the Manjaca camp. What he saw was a shed which, in better days, might have housed animals. Now it holds more than 600 men. Here the prisoners live, eat and sleep 24 hours a day. Most of these men just arrived three days ago from the camp at Omarska, their faces so haunted by memories they did not care to relate in the presence of their guards. For five minutes, Paddy Ashdown was allowed to speak privately to the men. However grim their conditions here, they told him, they are much better than in the place they've just come from. The camp commandant had promised Mr. Ashdown total freedom to see anything he wanted. In the end, he was told that wasn't possible. "Even during Mr. Ashdown's visit, time was limited to a mere half hour and access was limited to only a few prisoners. As he left, he said however bleak things seem to be, this camp did appear to be properly run. "Ashdown: Clearly, I have had access to those prisoners without the guards' presence. I detest their conditions. I find them deeply moving. They had an appalling time in Omarska where they've come from. I think it's a tremendous achievement on the part of the press to have exposed that, and they probably have saved many prisoners' lives. But every prisoner I spoke to here without the guards' presence has told me conditions are not what you'd want them to be but that they are a hell of a lot better in what they lived in before. "Reporter: With the visiting politician gone, what these men have suffered in the past remained largely unspoken. "... is a ... run camp in Serbian-held northern Bosnia. Authorities say they hold 3500 prisoners here, including about a thousand from the notorious Omarska camp. Pictures of emaciated captives in detention centres last week outraged the international community and prompted the Serbian leaders to quickly transfer hundreds to this military facility. "They are better ... "Reporter: This terrified looking prisoner mumbled that conditions here are slightly better. "There is, there is ... "Reporter: 'We get enough food now,' says this man. "We were only allowed to interview two inmates and, in each case, the soldiers immediately wanted to know what we would ask. "This is one of the camps that officials from the International Red Cross say they'll be inspecting this week. Indeed, the president of Bosnia's Serbs has offered to hand them control of all of these detention centres. The Serb leadership is under tremendous pressure to allow outsiders access to these camps. The proposed UN resolution will authorise any means necessary to implement that access, as well as guarantee the supply of humanitarian aid. Still, even though Karadzic himself authorised our visit to this camp, journalists were allowed less than half an hour to assess the situation. Soldiers moved us along rapidly, allowing us to take very few pictures and to ask even fewer questions. The camp commandant insists that the Geneva Conventions have been respected, but those prisoners we asked maintained they are civilians, not soldiers. Those we saw were crammed into cattle-sheds where they spend all day and all night, huddled together like animals. They are permitted to leave these quarters only briefly, for a small ration of bread and soup. "Christiane Amanpour, CNN, Manjaca, in northern Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have noticed that we have now English and French on the transcript. The B/C/S is in the subtitles. Only, Mr. Lukic, if there are any problems with the subtitling of the B/C/S then the Chamber, of course, would like to know, but that we have a complete record.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I haven't noticed that there was any problem. I was able to follow both B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's then -- Yes, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, was the footage in this recording from Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is a Manjaca camp. Of course, the inside is more important. The outside was shown in this movie.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Does this footage fairly and accurately depict Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: This footage, which is of very poor quality, does not show the real situation - but it was authentically filmed, that's true - because we cannot see here all the people. They were not all within the reach of the camera. We cannot see what they looked like. And even if this footage were of better quality, it would be very hard to recognise people because they had been largely exhausted by then, very emaciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll now ask Ms. Stewart to pause the clip at 38.1 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, although the quality of the picture is poor, do you recognise the person facing the camera on the right-hand side of the screen wearing the uniform?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Indubitably, this is Lieutenant-Colonel Bozidar Popovic, the camp commander, as they introduced him when we were there for talks. I can't say negotiations, because negotiations would imply an equal footing. Later for his service in this camp he was promoted into colonel, although he had been retired for three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I now tender this exhibit as the next Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document becomes Exhibit P157, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P157 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, I will now ask a few questions relating to the prisoners you met in Manjaca camp. In paragraph 10 of your 1996 statement, Prosecution Exhibit P154, e-court page 3, you describe talking with Omer Filipovic in the month before his death at the time of that first visit to Manjaca camp in June 1992. You state, I quote: "He informed me about what happened to them from the time when they were arrested. He gave me such a good report which made me convinced that he would not survive his stay in the camp but be killed." Mr. Medic, I would like to ask you one follow-up question on the quote from the statement I just read out. When Omer Filipovic told you about conditions in the camp, was anyone listening to him other than yourself?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: I had with me another three persons in the delegation. I don't know if I need to give you their names. And there were those officers standing there, the ones with whom we had talked and toured the barns. So Omer Filipovic gave me an account in their presence about all that happened between this registration hut where the prisoners are listed and how they lived without water, without bathroom, how they were beaten, sometimes randomly, sometimes picked individually, without any clothes, without any beds. I could see the traces of beating on Omer because there were blood-stains on his shirt, and he said all that before Colonel Tepsic, before Colonel Dikic , before Lieutenant-Colonel Bozidar Popovic, Lieutenant-Colonel Bosko Amidzic, and there was another officer whose name I cannot recall. They listened to his account the same as I. The others who were subordinated to them, the policemen or soldiers, whatever they were, were not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Medic, why did you believe that Omer Filipovic would be killed because of the report he gave you about Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: It was my feeling, my hunch, to put it that way, and, as I wrote in my report the next day, I felt that he would not shut up until they killed him. He was a policeman before the war. He was also an official of the municipality who was a teacher of history and geography. He was the president of a small party called MBO, I think, and he was a born leader who, in my mind, felt responsibility to say on behalf of all those people what was going on with them. He was physically and mentally healthy and strong, and his general attitude and the feeling of responsibility he had towards those people made him take it upon himself to say all these things. But I knew that such actions carry consequences, and I knew of his background before the war, and I was certain that he would not stop talking, that he would go on talking, and that he would be eventually killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, I'd now like to ask you some final questions about what you considered the purpose of Manjaca camp to be. In paragraph 21 of your 1996 statement, Exhibit P154, e-court page 5, you state: "On the 1st of August, 1992, Vukelic told me, facing the stables, that among the 2.000 prisoners in the camp, not even 200 had anything to do with the armed conflict." Mr. Medic, you made approximately 25 visits to Manjaca camp in 1992. We've heard that you spent nine years working for an association of camp inmates from that camp and you prepared a book collating their experiences. If Colonel Vukelic was correct in telling you that among 2.000 prisoners in the camp not even 200 had anything to do with the armed conflict, then based on your extensive experience of Manjaca camp, what conclusions were you able to draw about the purpose of imprisoning Bosnian and Croatian civilians in Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: On the morning of that day when Omer Filipovic was killed the night before, together with his friend, Bender --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that this asks for conclusions, and this gentleman, as I'm aware, is not an expert. So I would object to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm simply asking the witness for his factual observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's not what you did. But if that's what you intended to do, then please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I will rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, based on your factual observations of the camp, why were the Bosnian and Croatian civilians in Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: The official position of some officials in the Serb authorities was that no more than 5 per cent Muslims may remain. That was publicly stated. It's not my opinion. And for that purpose, it was necessary to cleanse the area from the Muslim and, later, the Croat population. In order to cleanse them -- and you can object to my observations all you want. In order to cleanse them, three things were done; namely, some were killed; some were imprisoned in camps; and yet others were driven out. To make these things easier, it was necessary to deprive these people of its leaders, to imprison Omer Filipovic and other intellectuals, either imprison them or kill them or expel them. It was necessary to eliminate people of renown. In small communities there are always prominent people, and these also needed to be removed. And, third, it was necessary to remove wealthy people who represented security in these small communities. So they were removed too. They were the first to be eliminated, either by imprisonment, killing or expulsion. The purpose, in my view, was to cleanse the area to eliminate Muslims and, later, Croats from these parts. I can look back to my own native Sanica. One in ten was killed; one in five was in Manjaca; and all the rest were expelled from Sanica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, perhaps it is unnecessary to remind you, but you are close to your 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I have no further questions at this time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Jeremy. Mr. Medic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for the Prosecution [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could I have a few seconds to consult with my client?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you could keep it to a minimum, please do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I hope you'll forgive me that it was a slip of the tongue that you're counsel for the Prosecution. Of course, you are counsel for the Defence, as Mr. Medic also will have understood. Mr. Medic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Lukic, counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Medic, good afternoon. I will put my questions in B/C/S and you will be answering in the same language, so please leave a short pause between question and answer for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have your statement before you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we turn to paragraph 5. You say: "Talic's demand meant, to me, that the army had taken responsibility for Manjaca camp." Was that the only proof at that time?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: At that moment, that was the only proof. But when I got to Manjaca, when Colonel Tepsic who had been sent by General Talic along with other officers there he said that it was a camp for prisoners of war under the command of the 1st Krajina Corps. And then it became quite clear that the army was in charge. If I may add my own comment, I believe this statement of his and all that passed between us made it impossible for us to get any further to Omarska and Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you about Omarska and Trnopolje later. You say in paragraph 8: "The kitchen prepared food that I believe never reached the prisoners." The prisoners ate, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to you, where did that food come from, if not from the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: When I made this observation I did not mean to imply that they were not eating at all. I meant to say they were not eating that food because I saw, and my father was a butcher, I saw meat being carved up, and I didn't think it was meant for the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When I'm waiting, it's not because I'm unhappy with your answer. I'm waiting for the interpretation. However, you had no insight into what the prisoners were actually eating.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Operatively, no; but, later on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 8 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just show in e-court 65 ter 13876.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This image, Mr. Medic, is related to one part of your statement. You say: Few of them had blankets. Most lay on the bare concrete floor. In this picture, as far as I can see, everyone, down to the last man, has a blanket. Did you go inside this facility?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Don't forget that I spent 15 days at the official inauguration of the camp, as Colonel Tepsic called it. The camp was opened on the 3rd of June, and I went there on the 18th. The situation then was that very few people had blankets. This picture was taken much later, I suppose. I know that one day the conditions were slightly improved, and they got some more supplies, including these blankets. I was talking only about when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we just agree that this photograph is not consistent with your statement in paragraph 8?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: I may agree, but this picture was taken later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I ask a question. Mr. Medic, can you point at the blankets that counsel says are there? I don't see them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we are looking at the same thing on the screen, you can see something of a different colour between the shoes -- and now the image disappeared. It's back. You can see that these are covers of some sort. I suppose that it was the ICRC, when they arrived, that brought them, and they came in the second half of July; that is to say, about a month after my stay at this camp. I was inside this facility only the first time and the last time. Never again. I hope I explained it well. You can see different colours. This is concrete between the shoes, and this here are blankets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you ask a witness whether something is inconsistent with his statement, wouldn't you agree with me that time can be quite relevant. And, therefore, what you see on the picture may be different from what the witness observed on this very specific day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, you're using this picture -- the Chamber, of course, in order to be able to follow your suggestion, there's an inconsistency, the Chamber would like to know when this picture was taken. Do we know?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't, Your Honour. The witness explained us that he entered only once. And when he entered, and it doesn't mean that the conditions were the same later on. So I think that the witness explained his knowledge, and I'm satisfied with that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Medic, in paragraph 9 of your statement, you say: "The injuries I observed on them were from beatings and bullets." You talk about the wounds you observed on the persons you saw at Manjaca. You have no medical training, do you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You had occasion to have private conversations with these people, without the presence of the guards?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Those were superficial conversations, especially with Mohammed Filipovic, who lay there immobile exclusively from beatings. He was the only one who was lying down in the entire hall. And the other person I mentioned, I know this by heart, was standing on his crutches with his leg bandaged and that was probably from a bullet. I talked to the other man, and his injuries were only from beatings. I'm certain about that. When the guard came in, no matter his rank, you had to stand up and put up your hands behind your head. That applied to the entire facility where the inmates were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll soon be going on a break. Let me just ask you this: Did you have occasion to speak with the prisoners privately without the presence of the guards?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: My interaction with Mohammed Filipovic was such that the officers who were present there could not hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, just for you to know, that the accused has been waving pieces of paper in the air with clear writing on it, one of it a year, a year within the time-frame of the Second World War, and some other years on it as well. The Chamber will consider whether and how it will respond to this. Make clear to your client that this is inappropriate behaviour which may have consequences. We first ask the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom. We'll take a break, and we'll be back in approximately 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we resume at 25 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The behaviour of Mr. Mladic I described just before the break was observed by one of the Judges. It was observed by security. It was observed by other staff as well. When I read out the behaviour before this break, Mr. Mladic nodded in the affirmative when I read it. It has happened today repeatedly. Showing text on paper readable from a distance, whether intended to be seen by Judges, by the public gallery, or to be caught by the cameras, while broadcasting these proceedings is inappropriate behaviour. The Chamber has decided that, as a measure of order, Mr. Mladic will be removed from the courtroom for the remainder of the testimony of the present witness. Please, curtains down. We take a break of one minute. And then we resume to hear the testimony of the witness. --- Break taken at 12.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Medic. The break took a bit longer. Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, can we go on now. We talked about the people that you spoke to in Manjaca. Were they dressed when they spoke so you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Of course they were not naked, but they were half-dressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sometimes we lawyers put questions that may --

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Seem strange to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. In the transcript at the Brdjanin trial on page 2262, 26th February, 2002, you were asked whether Mohammed Filipovic told you when it was that he had been beaten and your answer was no. Do you stand by that answer today?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When we talked about the type of food that the prisoners ate, I'd like to ask you something in relation to that, actually. At that time in Bosnia and Herzegovina, was there a general shortage of all vital supplies, like food, medicine, clothing?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: That was the very beginning of the war. In the Banja Luka region, there weren't any shortages yet, so, conditionally speaking, as far as that's concerned, life was normal from the point of view of food and clothing. There were already shortages of medicine though. For instance, I know that there was a problem getting medical alcohol at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time, were there shortages of water, gasoline, electricity, gas?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: No water shortages. Power cuts, well, sometimes they were intentional. Also, like there were these fictitious alarms. So this was part of the strategy. As General Talic said to me, You're a civilian, Adil, so you don't know about things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. We talked about paragraph 10 of your statement, and in relation to that, I'd like to ask you -- you speak about Omer Filipovic there as well and you corrected the date today. And you say that he was beaten to death with a baseball bat. What is your information based on?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Talking to inmates subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. In paragraph 11, you speak about finding the corpse of Omer Filipovic, and you say: "I was asked to be given a copy of the death certificate from the doctor at Manjaca, and also from a coroner. I was given the documents that I asked for but the man who gave them to me told me that I should not disclose that he had given me these documents. Dr. Sabanovic signed one of the death certificates." First, let me ask you this: Dr. Sabanovic, he is a Muslim, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes. A camp inmate at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A camp inmate at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: He signed the death certificate stating that the death had occurred but he did not state the cause of death. The pathological findings do disclose that, the ones that I got surreptitiously, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While we're on the subject can you tell us today who it was that gave you that document. We can even go into private session.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: I think that that is totally irrelevant. I received it at pathology. I couldn't have gotten it in the street, but as for the death certificates that's what I got at the command of the 1st Krajina Corps. I got it from their commission, so I got it at an official place, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You will allow for the fact that we have to check certain things through our own investigation, and that is why we need to have you confirm to us who gave you these papers so that we can establish whether that had actually happened.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: These pathological findings were taken out of my bag at the moment when I was arrested. I had a copy when I was arrested on the 1st of March, 1995. So whoever arrested me has the findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, we do not have these findings.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking you. Can you tell us who it was that gave you this.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: You're not going to gain anything by that because the man has been living abroad and, by the way, let me tell you that he's a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, whether Mr. Lukic gains anything by your answers or not is not the issue. He asked you whether he -- you could tell us who he was. If there's any need for you, for reasons to be explained by you, why you would give that name in private session, we would consider that. But you're invited to answer the question. And, again, if there's any reason why you think it should be dealt with confidentially, then we'll move into private session at your request.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally think that it's confidential because the man said to me that I shouldn't say how it was that I got that. I know the man. The man lives abroad. And he's been living abroad for a long time. He left as far as back at 1993. And I really think it is irrelevant who it was that gave me this, but I do claim that it does exist and that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, do you insist on an answer, in which case I would have to consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just provide one piece of information that might be useful to Mr. Lukic. I think it will also assist the Chamber. Dr. Sabanovic is a witness in this case. He is a 92 bis witness. If this is an issue Mr. Lukic wants to pursue, we could discuss whether that witness would be converted to 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does this assist you Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... obviously not the person who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... could we -- could we -- first of all, could we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Lukic, by the way, the Chamber has considered the loss of time which happened. The short breaks were in response to Mr. Mladic's request. Having looked at when that started, we'll continue without any further break until quarter past 2.00. And that comes close to two hours for you. If you would be able to conclude your cross-examination, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Medic, did you draft a report about that; and did you hand that report over at the Merhamet office?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: As an efficient person, or at least that's the way I saw myself, I made notes of everything that I saw and did. I drafted a report on five typed pages, and I delivered that to the Merhamet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can the documents still be found at the Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't know. The handwritten report was also taken from me. I didn't use a typewriter or a PC, so that handwritten report was taken away from me on the 1st of March, 1995, when I was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me come back to Omer Filipovic. In paragraph 11, you said that he was arrested as the president of the Muslim Bosniak organisation in Kljuc. We put it to you that he was arrested because he was the commander of the TO staff in Kljuc. On the 27th of May, 1992, the TO carried out an attack against non-armed soldiers on their way back from doing their compulsory military service. Three of them were killed. Six were seriously wounded. And 29 were slightly wounded on that occasion. Would you agree with me when I say that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: I can't say that I either agree or disagree. I don't know anything about that. I know what Omer did before the war, and I told you clearly and I can repeat that he was a history and geography teacher, that he was vice-president of the municipality as a volunteer, and he was also the president of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about that incident?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Subsequently I heard that there was a clash of some sort. However, I was declared unfit for military service. I did other things. I was not interested in the details of any of the things that had happened in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that on the same day, on the 27 May 1992, the unit under the command of Mr. Omer Filipovic killed the deputy commander of the public security station in Kljuc? Two policemen were wounded on that occasion, and all that happened in the sector of Krasulje village.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: I know that before the war, the commander of the police station in Kljuc was Mr. Atif Dzafic. I found him at Manjaca as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, but that was not an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In other words, you don't know?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that on that same day their armed units blew up the Banja Luka television repeater in Ramici village. Do you remember that your TV programme was cut?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Sir, please don't ask me anything about military matters because I really don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, then you just say, I don't know, and we'll move on. Thank you. Paragraph 12 in your statement, you say: "On the following day I saw Vukelic at Manjaca. He never mentioned that case, although I am convinced that he had known that those two persons were killed." That was your assumption. He never said anything about that, Vukelic, did he?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: It is true that I already had a very acute foreboding that something had happened at Manjaca. The guards behaved differently. They were quiet. They were subdued in their behaviour, and that's why I asked whether Colonel Vukelic was anywhere around and they told me to go to the barracks to see whether he was there. The entrance to the barracks was some 500 metres away from the entrance to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told me that he didn't say anything?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have to move on because our time is limited.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: However, subsequently, my impression was that he knew it. It was impossible that he didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you slow down between the two of you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 15, you talk about the composition of the delegation. On behalf of the Army of Republika Srpska, you mentioned Colonel Osman Selak. At that time Osman Selak was a member of the VRS. What was his rank?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: He was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was he subsequently actively involved in the work of Merhamet?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Not actively. However, we occasionally saw each other and he did come to Merhamet, but he was not an active member of -- of the organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the same paragraph, you say that Talic was a -- very pleasant in personal contacts. He always promised hell but he never delivered on those promises. At the Brdjanin trial to a Judge's question, you explained that you had in mind some other things, but when it came to the steps undertaken at Manjaca, when it comes to the delivery of humanitarian aid, all the promises and all the agreements were honoured. That is on transcript page 2277 on 26 of February 2002. Would you say the same thing today?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: I confirm and -- that I would say the same thing as I did at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 17, you speak about Omarska, and you say that General Talic never said that the army had anything to do with that. Since you carried out some investigations after that, could we agree today that General Talic's statement is correct, that the army had absolutely nothing to do with Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Since that was in the area of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps - and I'm speaking in military terms - it is my logic that things could not have been done unbeknownst to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the army control cities and villages or would it be the police who did that, if you know? If you don't know, never mind.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: If I just share my position with you, I would say that the police was the second-ranking force with respect to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. We're not going to discuss military issues. You said - we shouldn't anyway - I'm not going to answer.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 18 of your statement, you speak about the delivery of humanitarian aid. You organised that with the help of Merhamet. As far as I could tell, you went there once, and then there were 48 other deliveries of humanitarian aid. All in all, there were 49 deliveries of humanitarian aid by your organisation, by Merhamet to Manjaca. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We kept a book of visits, and we registered very correctly what things we delivered on each of those occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Every time you had to have a prior permission to deliver humanitarian aid, and you did receive it; right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Every time we had to receive a permission, but that doesn't mean that we received the permission on every application. That permit, or permission, was typewritten note - I have to slow down - and the wording on it was permit to move around the area of combat activities. The driver and all the escorts had to have their own permits issued to their names. Every time we went there, we had to apply. Every time we had to be given those permits from the command of the 1st Krajina Corps. We had to go to Colonel Bogovic, who was assistant chief for security. I believe we had to apply to the Department of Security or, rather, we had to go to a certain person called Dasic. I remember his family name very well because my neighbour's family name was also Dasici. He was also a junior officer. He was the one who dealt with us when we applied for those permits. Sometimes there were glitches and delays when issuing permits. And then, as a rule, Colonel Gojko Vujinovic would come on board to deal with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your activities improved the conditions at Manjaca; right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Of course. If you are in -- deep in mud, and if somebody offers you a stick to hold on to, then your situation does improve.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say in paragraph 19, which is the following paragraph: "I conveyed the information to -- about the three men from Kljuc who were killed on the 8th of August between Sedica [as interpreted] and Manjaca. Their names were Daut, whose family name is unknown; his brother; and Kemal, whose family name is unknown." Since then, have you learnt their full names?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Strangely enough, but Kemal worked in the catering company where I worked as the CEO. He was the head waiter. His alias was Kinanovic [phoen] but that was not his family name. That's just the name he went by. I don't remember his family name. I knew Daut personally and I didn't know his brother. Do you want me to explain how I arrived at their names?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only if you know their names. If not, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: There's a story to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just need their names. How you know them is not going to be of any assistance to me. Thank you. And now let's move on to paragraph 20 where you say that all the inmates under 18 and over 60 years of age were released from Manjaca, a total of 105 of them. In addition to that, people from Manjaca were released in August 1992. Are you aware of that? A group of them were -- was released. The International Committee of the Red Cross took them away.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: I know that. I did not participate in the events. Merhamet did not participate in the events either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, due to the fact that no pauses are made between question and answer, we have -- we are at risk that the transcript will not be accurate as who says what. Could you please -- "are you aware of," that your question, then I think it was the witness who said: "A group of them were released." Or was it your words?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I said it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said it. Yes, then I was a bit confused by putting a question and then adding some [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... inartfully posed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we only receive it, of course, by the interpretation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that 500 people were transferred to Batkovic in northern Bosnia. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Later on they were exchanged for Serbs imprisoned in Muslim and Croatian prisons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: The transfer of those approximately 500 people from Manjaca to Batkovici was the beginning of the end of Manjaca, of the disbanding of Manjaca. I believe that started on the 14th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well then.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: A large number of those people as I learned subsequently was successfully exchanged. The final exchange of 158 people from Manjaca was carried out in Travnik or a place near Travnik, in Turbe. I was present. I attended that exchange. The 158 people were exchanged together with 32 other people from Tunjice or Luka, I don't know where from. And that was on the 10th of October, 1993. So, in other words, those people had spent a year and a half in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Of course, you don't know how much time did the people spend in prison who were on the other side?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: From where I was standing, I could only tell that they were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did that exchange take place, once again?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: At Turbe. There were buses. One would group would leave a bus and would get on the other bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was in October?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was on the 10th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 21, the last two sentences. The first words are: "I was aware of only one professional soldier who -- who was kept prisoner at Manjaca." When we're talking about that, do you know that there was fighting in the municipality of Prijedor? We did say that we would not discuss military matters but this is a notorious fact. That's why I'm asking you about it.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're not talking about that one individual. When we're talking about the fact that there were no --

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: I had information about general suffering, but I didn't have any specific information. The first such place was Srebrenica, so I didn't know anything about any individuals being killed or suffering.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 24, you speak about the prison in Stara Gradiska, and you say that the 1st Krajina Corps most probably used that prison as well. Do you know that the prison in Gradiska -- when you are talking about that prison, are you referring to the prison in Gradiska in Croatia or Gradiska in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Which one?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: The prison in Stara Gradiska is in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then we will not discusses that at all.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: However, people from the territory of Kljuc before they arrived at Manjaca, a certain number of them had spent time at Stara Gradiska. Among them, Hilmo, who cut his own throat when he saw what he looked like in the mirror. He had spent some time in Stara Gradiska and then Manjaca was opened, and then he was transferred to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He inflicted injuries on himself. However, four days later, when he left the hospital -- what hospital was that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: The clinical hospital at Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you read the transcript, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked you where he was hospitalised, and operated on. Your answer was not recorded. Could you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: In Banja Luka. There are two hospitals in Banja Luka. One is the so-called old hospital and the other is the so-called new hospital. But both facilities belong to the Clinical Hospital Centre. He slit his throat at the old hospital and he was surgically treated in the new hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 28, you speak about Ljubija. In the territory of the Ljubija local commune is it correct that the majority of the population were Croats?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I know that Donja Ljubija, also known as Islam, is mostly populated by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When I say the local commune of Ljubija, I also imply the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Of course, but I don't know. I only know that Islam is an exclusively Muslim neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know, although this is again a military issue, that Croats in that area joined the ranks of the VRS en masse?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: If they did that, I'm sure they did not do that of their own will because I know for a fact because I travelled with a priest who served near Ljubija. A month or so later, he was found dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What's the priest's name?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: I don't know his name, but I know that there was another priest who worked in the Caritas office in Banja Luka. His name was Martanovic [phoen]. And there was another priest who was found dead drowned in a well together with his parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When we are talking about the voluntarily nature of the unit that comprised all Croats, those units were armed. Can you really say that somebody took up arms voluntarily? People served in their own homes. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 33, you speak about Koricanske Stijene. Do you know with whom the perpetrators of the killing at Koricanske Stijene were affiliated? Do you know that they were members of the police?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Prijedor police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the survivors of that killing were found by members of the army and taken to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: I know that, but I know equally well that the investigating judge who had come up on the site to investigate was removed by the troops. The name of the lawyer is Jankovic. He is a now a lawyer in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 37, you speak about the arrest of members of Merhamet. This arrest, just as the investigation that followed, was carried out by the police?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes. But we were turned over to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were at Mali Logor?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, military prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The prisoners there were mostly Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Yes, Serb criminals and Serb murders who were under investigation. Of course, the life of Serbs in that camp was very different to the lives of Muslims and the few Croats who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us now turn to paragraph 49 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Sadika Ceric.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So there were women there too. She told you that if Banja Luka were to be attacked, the prison would be closed and all non-Serb prisoners shot. Did Sadika Ceric tell you from whom she had heard that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: No. But the position of the cells, the layout of the cells was such that one could often hear conversations between guards in the hallway, especially those who were in Sanica. Sanica did not have windows. It had a wooden door and bars, and the door would often be left ajar because there was no natural light, nor air. She had that that way, and she told me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So she didn't know who was speaking?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are wrapping up. I won't be straining your patience much longer. Do you know that the Supreme Court of Republika Srpska brought in a verdict convicting, Zeljko Bulatovic, Sinisa Teodorovic, and Zoran Gajic for their participation in the beatings of people at Manjaca and their involvement in the killings of Omer Filipovic, and, help me, who was with him?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Esad Bender.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: I know there was a trial, but I don't know the outcome. But I know very well who Bulatovic is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, this was all I had for you today. Thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. In order to avoid any problems in the future, Mr. Lukic, you referred to paragraph 49 when you mentioned that Sadika Ceric had heard that if Banja Luka was attacked, the prison would be closed and all Serb prisoners shot. Now, in the version which we have in e-court it is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... 50. I thought it was 50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh -- let me see. Yes, it is on the transcript as 49, I think. Yes. So.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no -- that's a possibility. The only thing I wanted to avoid for the future is that your private numbering is different from the numbering by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I tried to use their numbering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's try to do that from now on. Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Jeremy -- I first consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, your mike is on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, in paragraph 50, it doesn't say Serb prisoners would be killed, but non-Serb prisoners would be killed. That's an essential difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I misspoke, then apologies for that. But that's actually what paragraph 50 says. The Judges have no further questions for you. Mr. Jeremy, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, on temporary transcript page 64, you were asked how many times you personally visited Manjaca camp. Just so that your answer is clear, I would like to ask you again how many times you personally visit the Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: The first 15 times, I went every time, trying to introduce my associates so they can go alone, and the other times, I accompanied them once in two or three times. So, all in all, it was a total of 25 visits. But the first 15 visit, I always went.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, in cross-examination, you were asked about your arrest on temporary transcript page 70. You referred to your arrest on -- in paragraphs 37 to 52 of your statement where you describe the arrest and imprisonment in early 1995 of various of the senior leadership of Merhamet, including yourself. Very briefly, in a few words, what were you charged with?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Only the leadership of Merhamet was arrested, the top five people. I was arrested the next day because I no longer belonged to the leadership by that time. We were charged with spying. After those arrested in Sanski Most, Prijedor and Banja Luka, the youngest was 42 and the oldest was 72. In terms of gender and age, the people were mixed. Those from Sanski Most and Prijedor were taken to court six times, but no verdict was brought in. We, from Banja Luka, were brought before court three times, but the trial never called it -- never took place. They always found a way to postpone it, and the people in those white uniforms were there, I believe from some international organisation. Maybe that was the reason. But, at any rate, we were charged with espionage that had never been proven.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And to be clear, neither you nor any of the senior leadership of Merhamet were convicted?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody was convicted, neither us from Banja Luka, nor the other people from Sanski Most and Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: A final question, Mr. Medic. What impacts did the arrest and imprisonment of the senior leadership of Merhamet have on the non-Serb civilian population that remained in Banja Luka in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ADIL MEDIC
utterances.text: Our arrests were consistent with what we discussed earlier, the cleansing of non-Serbs from various areas; in our case, the region of Banja Luka. In fact, those people who remained until 1995 were left there with the intention of not leaving Banja Luka ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Moloto would like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, if you could just listen to the question by the lawyer. The question was: What impact did the imprisonment of the senior leadership of Merhamet have on the population that remained in Banja Luka in 1995. If you can just answer to that, that would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After our arrests, not a single convoy left Banja Luka or the Banja Luka region again to get assistance, and that was a very effective way to get the rest of the population to move out, because, as we said before, there were deficits of everything. No more supplies got in and no more letters. We used to bring them before, of course, checked by the Serbian authorities. So the rest of the population moved out. That was the result of our arrests. Not a single convoy - I repeat - left again after our arrests.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jeremy. Mr. Lukic, the questions in re-examination have not triggered any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this concludes your testimony, Mr. Medic, in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for answering all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic, there is one matter outstanding which the Chamber would prefer you to address, if you want to address it at all, in an oral submission on Monday. And that is the issue of the administrative schedule of meetings as proposed by Mr. Groome. I do not know whether you want to at all address the matter further or whether you just agree or --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In essence we don't oppose, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't oppose. So if you want to make any further submissions on that, then we'd like to hear from you on Monday because the Chamber would prefer to adjourn for the day. The removal of Mr. Mladic from the courtroom was during the remainder of the testimony of this witness. That means that we expect Mr. Mladic to be back on Monday morning at 9.30. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Nothing from the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing from the Prosecution. And nothing from the Defence. Then we adjourn for the day and we will resume on Monday, the 3rd of September, at 9.30 in the morning, I think it will be in this same courtroom, I. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 3rd day of September, 2012, at 9.30 a.m. 22 23 24 25
